title: the Gayatri in context
hook: the verse everyone calls the Gayatri never says the word gayatri. so where did the name come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: Savitr, the golden-handed god who stirs the day awake and, at evening, lets the weaver roll up her cloth. What did you roll up and leave for today? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.
screen: `THE ONE WHO STIRS, AND THE ONE WHO STILLS.`

segments.voice: Here's a small puzzle. Say the verse through, from tat savitur to prachodayat, and listen for the word gayatri. It isn't there. The verse names Savitr. It names the god's radiance. It asks for thoughts to be stirred. It never once names itself. And yet, in everyday speech, it goes by the Gayatri. A name like that had to come from somewhere outside the words. Today: where the name comes from, and the other name the verse goes by.
screen: `LISTEN FOR THE WORD GAYATRI.` → `IT ISN'T THERE.` → `SO WHERE DID THE NAME COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Gayatri is the name of a meter. A meter is the shape of a verse: how many lines it has and how many syllables fill each line. In Vedic tradition, the gayatri meter is counted as three lines of eight syllables each. Short lines. Three of them. You can hear the shape in the verse itself: tat savitur varenyam, one line. Bhargo devasya dhimahi, a second. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, a third. Three steps, and done. So this verse is called by the name of the vessel it's poured into. It's a bit like calling a poem a sonnet, except that, over time, this one verse became so central that its meter's name became its own. The shape isn't rare to this verse. The hymn that opens the whole Rig Veda, to Agni, the fire, is set in the same meter. Generations of reciters carried these short three-line verses in their mouths. And the verse has a second name. Older law books, like the Manusmriti, call it the Savitri: the verse to Savitr, named for the god it speaks to rather than for its shape. Two names, two ways of seeing the same lines. One looks at the form: three short lines that are easy to carry. The other looks at the address: who the lines are spoken to. Later tradition went further and honored Gayatri herself as a goddess, the verse become a presence. But under every layer sits a plain fact. Gayatri is a shape, a rhythm a person can hold one breath at a time.
screen: `THE VERSE NEVER SAYS "GAYATRI."` · `GAYATRI: THE NAME OF A METER.` · `THREE SHORT LINES.` · `ALSO CALLED THE SAVITRI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a verse with no words, only its shape. Sit, and let the breath slow. On the next out-breath, count eight in your head, slowly, one count per beat. That's one line. Breathe in. Count eight again on the out-breath. That's the second line. And once more: the third. Three short lines. Then rest for a few natural breaths, and begin again. If you lose count, start the line over. Nothing is said, nothing is chanted, but you're holding the shape the verse is named for. The bell holds the time.
The Gayatri in context. Gayatri is the name of a meter, three short lines, and the verse took its name. In older law books it's the Savitri, named for its god. Today's word.

Your line: the Gayatri in context. Today, notice one thing named for its shape rather than its content, a sonnet, a haiku, a three-line text, and think of the verse named for its meter. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: In Vedic recitation, students learn the meters of the hymns along with their words; the Gayatri is learned both as a verse and as an example of the gayatri meter, and in older texts it is often called the Savitri.

fork.setup: the verse doesn't name itself. you're reading an older law book like the Manusmriti. what does it call the verse?
fork.reveal: the Savitri, after Savitr, the god it speaks to. the name Gayatri comes from its meter.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of a Vedic meter of three short lines, which became the name of the verse in it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gayatri is the name the verse gives itself.
what it means: gayatri is a meter, and the verse took the meter's name; older texts also call it the Savitri.
what a scholar hears: tradition counts eight syllables a line, and reciters often sound varenyam as va-re-ni-yam, a syllable longer than it is written.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.1 (the hymn to Agni, in gayatri meter)

notes: The gayatri meter as three padas of eight syllables is attributed to tradition ('Vedic tradition counts'); confirm.
Claim that Rig Veda 1.1 is in gayatri meter: from memory; confirm.
Manusmriti's use of 'savitri' for the verse (around 2.77–2.83, 2.101–2.104): from memory; confirm the verse range.
Trapdoor: the reading va-re-ni-yam to fill out the line is a widely noted point about the meter but is stated here from memory; confirm or cut.
'The shape isn't rare to this verse' rests on the Agni example only.
Gayatri honored as a goddess: also said on day 108; standard but general.
